# Gospel of Thomas, Saying 14 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Nag Hammadi Codex II, p. 34 | **Source Image:** source-texts/coptic/GTH_014_page_001.jpg

---

## Saying 14

**1** Jesus said to them: "If you fast, you will bring sin upon yourselves.

**2** If you pray, you will be condemned.

**3** If you give alms, you will harm your spirits.

**4** When you go into any land and travel through the countryside, if they receive you, eat what they set before you, and heal the sick among them.

**5** For what goes into your mouth will not defile you. Rather, what comes out of your mouth — that is what will defile you."

---

**Consensus Notes (SOPHIA):**

**Vv.1-3** — LOGOS/EMET preferred. The absolute negation of fasting, prayer, and almsgiving is the most radical statement in the collection. PNEUMA's present-tense "you are sinning" is arguably more accurate but the future tense of LOGOS follows Coptic construction better.

**"Harm your spirits"** — LOGOS preferred over PNEUMA's "damage your inner selves." *Pneuma* in Coptic is the spirit-self, a technical term worth preserving.

**V.4** — consensus. The positive instruction: receive hospitality, eat without restriction, heal. This is the Thomas version of the missionary charge (cf. Luke 10:8-9).

**V.5** — consensus. "Defile" preserved over PNEUMA's "make unclean" — they are equivalent but "defile" is the established English purity-law term.

**Synoptic Parallels:**
- V.4: Luke 10:8-9 (missionary charge — eat what is set before you; heal the sick) — very close parallel
- V.5: Mark 7:15 / Matt 15:11 (purity saying) — Thomas's formulation is starker and lacks Mark's allegorical elaboration
- Vv.1-3 have no Synoptic parallel; they represent Thomas's anti-ritual stance at its sharpest
